iterations.theme: Political contrarianism, ecological consensus, and economic protectionism

sections.subtitle: Searching for a civilizational minimum in a polarized society
sections.screenshot_description: Marin Marić introduces guest Petar Šarić and opens the topic of political pluralism in the studio
sections.content:
In the 115th edition of the podcast of the association *Mladi za domovinu*, host Marin Marić hosted Petar Šarić, philosopher, sociologist, doctoral student at the Faculty of Arts in Ljubljana, and president of the World Youth Alliance and the association Atlas Hrvatska. The occasion for the conversation was the increasingly pronounced degradation of public and political discourse in Croatia, where despite the apparent wealth of pluralism and the constant emergence of new political options, substantive debate is absent.

Marić observes how the domestic political scene in every election cycle faces a flood of new parties, but instead of a mature confrontation of arguments, the public space becomes poisoned by base passions and mutual discreditations. The goal of the discussion was to detect the civilizational minimum — the fundamental assumptions around which political actors, regardless of worldview differences, would have to agree so that genuine pluralism could function at all. In this, it is not a matter of creating unnatural coalitions, but of defining a safe framework within which legitimate political struggles can be waged without jeopardizing the common good.

sections.subtitle: The trap of contrarianism: Renouncing principles for the sake of political comfort
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić analyzes the loss of worldview consistency and the phenomenon of political contrarianism
sections.content:
As a starting point for the analysis of the crisis of ideas, Marin Marić cited Petar Šarić's column in which the erosion of worldview consistency in the era of mass media is addressed. In a world oversaturated with information and propaganda manipulations, political actors increasingly abandon their own principles in order to position themselves exclusively as the negation of the opposing side. Šarić defines this phenomenon as the syndrome of political postmodernity, a period in which 'grand narratives' have disappeared, and voters and politicians have lost firm worldview orientation points.

Due to such dynamics, absurd situations arise in which someone defends a certain thesis one day, and already ten days later advocates a completely opposite one — merely because in the meantime the original proposal came from the camp of political opponents. Marić and Šarić cite concrete examples from the domestic scene: from reactions to the investments of musician Marko Perković Thompson on the left, to the automatic criticism of every infrastructural move of the Zagreb city government by the right. Šarić emphasizes that in politics it is necessary to have intellectual and psychological courage to acknowledge the objective good, regardless of who is implementing it at a given moment.

sections.subtitle: The Foucaultian understanding of politics: Power instead of objective truth
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains the influence of Michel Foucault's philosophy on modern politics
sections.content:
Entering deeper into the theoretical causes of such behavior, Petar Šarić refers to the French post-structuralist philosopher Michel Foucault and his concept of the politics of power. According to Foucault's view, in the social and political field there is no objective truth nor universal good; there exist exclusively opposing camps of power that seek to impose their own particular interests as universally valid truth. In such a system, victory in discourse does not depend on the groundedness of arguments, but on the accumulation of power necessary for domination.

Šarić warns that contemporary political contrarianism is a direct fruit of such philosophy. When the existence of objective values is rejected, the question of the well-being of society and citizens ceases to be important, and the sole goal becomes thwarting the rival camp. Although such an approach originally belongs to a radical left paradigm, Šarić observes that today in practice it has been adopted by many nominally right-wing options as well, whereby political life is reduced to mere affective polarization driven by emotions instead of principles.

sections.subtitle: Environmental protection is not a monopoly of the green left: Toward an anthropocentric ecology
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić argues why environmental protection must be based on human dignity
sections.content:
As the first key point of potential consensus, the interlocutors opened the topic of ecology. Marin Marić posed the question of how nature protection — a universal question of survival — became almost the exclusive political brand of the green left. Šarić recalls the historical development from the hippie movement of the 1960s through the eighties and nineties, when green initiatives entered institutional spheres of power and branded the ecological narrative through the prism of imminent cataclysm.

However, the fundamental philosophical problem of the green left's approach lies in biocentrism and a kind of animistic revival of the concept of 'Mother Earth' (Gaia), where nature is viewed as a self-valuable system in which man is often reduced to a 'pest' or a mere carbon footprint. Šarić warns that such an ontology leads into a culture of death, including demands for depopulation. In contrast, Šarić advocates a healthy anthropocentric approach: man possesses inalienable human dignity, and nature is entrusted to him for stewardship. Care for clean air, water, and soil is therefore not a leftist whim, but an essential duty of preserving resources for future generations.

sections.subtitle: Scruton's oikophilia and subsidiarity: The local community ahead of global decrees
sections.screenshot_description: The guest explains the difference between a 'bottom-up' approach and globalist regulations
sections.content:
In the continuation of the discussion, Marin Marić looked back at the work of the renowned British conservative philosopher Roger Scruton and his concept of *oikophilia* — an innate love of home that encompasses family, tradition, community, and the belonging environment. Šarić clarifies that the principle of subsidiarity, taken from the social teaching of the Church, is based on this idea, according to which care for the environment primarily belongs to local communities. People who live in a particular area know its value best and have a natural motivation to preserve it.

The main clash between the conservative and the contemporary left-liberal green approach manifests itself in the method of action. While the left prefers centralized, global 'top-down' regulations imposed by international institutions, there is a danger that such decrees — under the influence of corporate lobbies — will destroy the livelihoods of small farmers and local communities (such as bans on cattle farming to reduce methane emissions).

Šarić recalls the historical rift in the First International between Karl Marx and Mikhail Bakunin, noting that today, too, a battle is being waged between bureaucratic centralization and local autonomy. As a solution, he offers a model in which umbrella institutions define the framework, but give full freedom to those who have real risk in the process — a concept that Americans call *skin in the game*.

sections.subtitle: Nuclear energy in the rift between ideology and the sociology of risk
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the sociology of risk and prejudices toward nuclear energy
sections.content:
As a glaring example of ideological blindness and contrarianism, the interlocutors highlight the question of nuclear energy. Although it is a clean, highly efficient energy source with a negligible carbon footprint, the green left harbors deep distrust toward it. Šarić recalls the protests of the association Zelena akcija in Zagreb against the plans of the Ministry of Economy for the development of nuclear projects, which he considers absurd in the context of the proclaimed fight against fossil fuels.

As a sociologist, Šarić explains the phenomenon of fear of nuclear energy through the theory of the sociology of risk. The human perception of danger is not based on mathematical probability, but is culturally and media-constructed. Pop culture, disaster movies, and sensationalist media create a hyperinflation of fear of unlikely events — such as nuclear disasters or black holes created at CERN — while real, everyday risks are ignored. Thus, for example, the risk of dying in automobile traffic is statistically incomparably greater than flying by airplane, just as harmless spiders are a source of greater fear than mosquitoes that transmit deadly diseases.

sections.subtitle: Ecological consensus: A commonsense debt to ancestors and descendants
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić summarizes the ecological responsibility of the right toward future generations
sections.content:
At Marić's prompting to summarize the ecological topic from the perspective of center-right and conservative voters, Petar Šarić articulated the principle of intergenerational solidarity. He pointed out that generations born in the twentieth century grew up enjoying the benefits of unpolluted nature — from drinking clean water from the tap and consuming homegrown produce to spending carefree time in forests and rivers.

That historical heritage, which previous generations defended for centuries, imposes a moral obligation to preserve resources and hand them down to descendants in equal or better condition. Šarić underlines that the protection of the natural environment must not be subordinated to calculations about short-term GDP growth nor to the greed of individuals who turn domestic space into foreign waste dumps. Ecological responsibility must be depoliticized and recognized as a fundamental patriotic reflex, freed from the need for constant conflict with those who think differently.

sections.subtitle: Corporate dictate and the necessity of healthy economic protectionism
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić unpacks the influence of big capital on the real estate market and domestic production
sections.content:
The second major point of necessary political consensus, according to Petar Šarić's assessment, refers to recognizing the negative effects of corporate power on the lives of citizens. Although criticism of corporations was traditionally considered a prerogative of the left, Šarić recalls the concept of crony capitalism (*crony capitalism*), which the contemporary right also recognizes. Under the conditions of a globalized market, transnational conglomerates dispose of capital greater than the budgets of many states, thereby acquiring the power to directly dictate social and economic flows.

In order to protect its own people, the state must implement healthy economic protectionism in three key domains:

- **Goods market:** It is necessary to actively support local food producers who cannot compete price-wise with mass imports of dubious quality laden with pesticides.
- **Capital and real estate market:** It is essential to introduce restrictions so that foreign investment funds do not buy up entire city quarters (such as examples in Zagreb), turning real estate into speculative capital and thus preventing young Croatian families from acquiring their own home.
- **Freedom of movement of people:** The uncontrolled influx of cheap labor lowers the price of labor and creates long-term social risks, which directly opens the question of regulating migration flows.

iterations.theme: Demographics, migration, national security, and Croatia's role in Europe

sections.subtitle: The question of migration and the economic motivation for importing foreign labor
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains how importing labor is not a moral act but an argument of economic utility.
sections.content:
In the continuation of the conversation, Marin Marić opens one of the hottest political and social questions of today – migration, demographics, and the importation of foreign labor. The host observes that precisely this topic will dominate future election cycles and poses the question of whether there is a possibility of minimal consensus around it.

Petar Šarić points out that the debate on migration in Croatia has experienced a kind of ideological paradox. While from the classical economic right one would expect advocacy of an open market, in the Croatian context the right is skeptical toward it, while the left spectrum often resorts to moralistic discourse in order to justify the importation of workers due to market needs. Šarić emphasizes that behind the importation of foreign labor there is actually no sublime moral concern for those people, but exclusively an **argument of economic utility**.

It is, the guest explains, an attempt to artificially keep unsustainable systems alive, such as the existing pension model or achieving short-term profit for employers through cheaper services. He considers it absurd to expect a foreign worker to arrive with the mission of saving the Croatian pension system. If citizens were asked in a referendum about importing foreign labor, Šarić believes that the majority would reject such a model and choose abstinence from the mass importation of workers.

sections.subtitle: Questioning the concept of integration and the real need for labor
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić uses the metaphor of digging a pit with spoons instead of an excavator to illustrate the illusion of the need for labor.
sections.content:
Discussing the legal status of foreign workers and the acquisition of citizenship, Petar Šarić distinguishes mere legal form from actual belonging to a people. Touching upon terms that dominate the public space, the guest warns that concepts such as 'need for labor' and 'integration' have become mystical phrases that resolve little.

Šarić poses a provocative question: does an objective need for so much labor really exist, or is it a socially conditioned illusion? To illustrate this, he offers a vivid example: if ten thousand workers dig a deep pit with small spoons, the impression of an enormous need for manpower is created, whereas one excavator would do the same job faster, cheaper, and more efficiently. The problem lies in the fact that employers often prefer to rely on the simple accumulation of cheap workers rather than on innovation and a more rational organization of business.

When it comes to the famous concept of integration, Šarić from a sociological perspective openly acknowledges that in science there is actually **no consensus** on when someone is truly integrated – is it the moment they learn the language, start cheering for the national team, or forget their native language. History shows that different peoples have truly connected and integrated almost exclusively under the pressure of a common enemy in wartime circumstances, which is certainly not a scenario anyone would wish for in peacetime.

sections.subtitle: Technological progress, automation, and the long-term consequences of importing workers
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the contradiction between announcements of automation and the mass importation of workers.
sections.content:
The interlocutors reflect on the obvious contradiction of the modern era: on the one hand, the media daily announce that artificial intelligence and automation will eliminate jobs, while on the other hand, it is claimed that there is an inexhaustible hunger for physical labor. Šarić points out that the idea of an unlimited need for workers is an ideological construct that ignores technological progress.

Marin Marić recalls that automation is in the long term always more cost-effective than cheap labor, but poses the key question: what will happen to so much accumulated foreign labor when technology takes over their jobs? Šarić warns that the political elites, who made the decision on the uncontrolled opening of borders, consciously ignored the known negative consequences. Among them are:

- the creation of ghettos and parallel societies,
- an increase in insecurity and tensions among the local population,
- the erosion of social cohesion.

The guest emphasizes that foreign workers themselves are not malicious; most of them come for material reasons in search of a better life and earnings for their families. The blame lies with decision-makers who placed short-term GDP growth and the interests of capital ahead of the long-term stability and destiny of their own people.

sections.subtitle: Labor rights of foreign workers and the fundamental question of human dignity
sections.screenshot_description: The guest analyzes the difference between transcendent human dignity and international human rights.
sections.content:
Marin Marić proposes a potential point of political consensus: insisting on strict labor rights and dignified conditions for foreign workers. If employers were legally obligated to ensure equal wages, quality accommodation, and high labor standards, the economic motive for importing cheap labor would largely weaken.

Petar Šarić supports that idea and deepens the discussion with a philosophical reflection on the difference between **human dignity** and **human rights**. He explains that the political left prefers the concept of human rights because it perceives them as a product of international conventions and legal agreements. However, the danger of such an approach lies in the fact that what has been created by convention, those in power can also abolish or redefine by convention.

In contrast, human dignity has a transcendent, God-given character that surpasses every temporal authority and state. Šarić emphasizes that human dignity must be the foundation and prerequisite from which human rights stem, and not the other way around. He concludes that economic advancement and mild GDP growth cannot justify the exploitation of people from the third world nor the endangering of the fundamental sense of security of domestic citizens.

sections.subtitle: Security consensus: investing in the armed forces and state stability
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains the necessity of consensus regarding investment in the military in a world of growing geopolitical instabilities.
sections.content:
In a time of declining global security and growing multipolarity, the interlocutors move to the topic of the armed forces. Marin Marić points out that the issue of defense and the military should be spared daily political squabbling, whereby debate should be allowed to exist regarding modalities (such as the introduction of military service), but not regarding the strengthening of defense capacities itself.

Petar Šarić strongly supports this thesis, emphasizing that security requires long-term rationality. If a state does not invest in its own defense, it cannot expect stability in a world where the unipolar order is weakening before the challenges of powers like Russia or China. The guest observes a paradox within a part of the left: although they enjoy all the civilizational advantages of the existing order, they often obstruct military investments that alone can defend that order.

Šarić recognizes a similar paradox in the migration policy of the green left. It uncritically encourages the arrival of populations whose worldviews and cultural values are often in direct conflict with the fundamental postulates promoted by that same left, ignoring the real security and social risks of such policies.

sections.subtitle: Production self-sufficiency, energy independence, and demographic survival
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about energy self-sufficiency and strategic planning in the context of demographic changes.
sections.content:
Speaking about the foundations of long-term security, Petar Šarić broadens the concept of defense to production and energy sustainability. He warns of the excessive dependence of the Croatian economy on tourism. Although tourism currently generates enormous revenues, the key question is what that capital is invested into. Instead of passivity, resources must be redirected into strategic projects that guarantee energy independence, such as nuclear energy.

The guest then touches upon the painful question of demographics. Although everyone would like to see a reversal of negative demographic trends and a rise in the birth rate, Šarić calls for strategic realism and poses an uncomfortable question: what if Croatia in a few decades has significantly fewer inhabitants? In order for the people to survive in such circumstances, the state must build three key pillars in time:

1. Its own and stable energy production,
2. A strong and equipped military,
3. Self-sufficient local production of basic goods and food.

Only when a small community has these prerequisites secured can it weather historical demographic crises and preserve sovereignty until some better times.

sections.subtitle: The geopolitical position of Croatia: criticism of Western weaknesses and misconceptions about alternatives
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić criticizes misconceptions about the Russian or Chinese alternative and advocates a clear stance within the West.
sections.content:
To Marin Marić's question about Croatia's geopolitical orientation in a world that is becoming multipolar, Petar Šarić offers a sober analysis of the country's position within Euro-Atlantic integration. He acknowledges that the contemporary West suffers from severe ideological decadence and erroneous migration policies that destroy its urban environments, which the European bureaucracy often uncritically pushes.

Nevertheless, he rejects cheap contrarianism that, due to the shortcomings of the West, seeks salvation in illusions about Russia or China. Šarić recalls that Russia is by no means a model of a traditional society, given high rates of divorce, abortion, and the enduring legacy of Soviet socialism. On the other hand, the Western civilizational and security framework (NATO and the EU) provides an incomparably higher quality of life, freedom, and international standing to citizens.

The solution, therefore, is not abandoning the European framework, but rejecting the servile mentality. Croatian politicians, Šarić believes, on the international scene must learn to say 'no' to policies that harm national interests, instead of uncritically and spinelessly accepting all directives coming from Brussels.

sections.subtitle: Croatia as a historical bulwark and moral corrective of the European continent
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić emphasizes Croatia's historical role as a warrior caste and moral remedy for Europe.
sections.content:
Marin Marić recalls Croatia's historical status as the bulwark of Christianity (*Antemurale Christianitatis*) and poses the question of why a feeling of inferiority is created in society and European belonging is treated exclusively through monetary transactions, funds, and bureaucratic orders.

Petar Šarić responds with a powerful vision of Croatia's role in contemporary Europe. Croatia is not a peripheral and small country that needs to sit at the table with bowed head and beg Paris or Berlin for technology and guidelines. Croats were historically the **warrior caste of Europe** and its defenders at key moments in history — from centuries of resistance to the Ottoman Empire to the defense of their own freedom:

> „Mi smo lijek za Europu. Mi smo ono što Europi u ovom trenutku treba... Naša uloga nije da samo sjedimo za stolom, naša uloga je da vodimo glavnu riječ za stolom i podsjetimo ih na temeljne principe koje su očito zaboravili.”

Since the Croatian people have to a great extent preserved commitment to Christian values, family, and patriotism, Šarić holds that Croatia has a moral duty to act as a corrective to a faltering Europe, rather than adopting its destructions.

sections.subtitle: Three fundamental points of political consensus and the importance of personal responsibility
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić summarizes three unquestionable points of national consensus for all political actors.

sections.subtitle: Concluding thoughts on healthy pluralism and sign-off from the show
sections.screenshot_description: Marin Marić concludes the 115th episode of the podcast with a message about genuine pluralism and a common national framework.
sections.content:
At the very close, host Marin Marić thanks the guest for an inspiring and deep conversation, emphasizing that Petar Šarić once again justified his status as one of the most prominent young Croatian intellectuals.

Marić concludes the episode with a reflection on the true nature of the democratic order. True pluralism does not imply the false assumption that all opinions and all values are equally good, nor does it require political opponents to trample their convictions for the sake of apparent unity. The purpose of healthy pluralism is the existence of different philosophies and ideas that compete freely, but exclusively within a clearly established, unquestionable framework of the common national and human interest.

With that message about the need to define the common foundations of Croatia's future, Marić thanks the viewers and signs off from the 115th edition of the podcast of the association Mladi za domovinu.
